purpose: A bounded method by which an independent business-email and cloud reseller moves a small business from its existing mail and file estate into a correctly architected, security-baselined tenant: deciding the documented authorization and least-privilege access model, the tenant and identity layout whose creation-time choices cannot be undone, the domain and DNS control plus mail-authentication design that keeps mail delivering, the migration method and the honest data-scope and fidelity statement it implies, the timed cutover with a proven rollback position, and the user communication, training, stabilization, as-built documentation and acceptance that end the project cleanly without interrupting the client's business or exceeding the access the client granted.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

the operator is a small independent reseller delivering a business suite (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace or a comparable platform) to small businesses, typically single-tenant engagements from a handful to a few dozen seats

administrative access to a client tenant is granted by the client in writing, exercised under least privilege, and revocable by the client at any time; the client owns the tenant, its domains and its data throughout

vendor plan capabilities, feature names, retention windows, enforcement defaults and delegated-administration mechanisms change over time, so every mechanism described here must be re-verified against the vendor's current documentation for the client's specific plan at build time

privacy, records-retention and sector-specific obligations vary by jurisdiction and industry; this KB names obligation classes only and assumes the operator verifies current rules in their own jurisdiction
the content is educational operating knowledge for the reseller and not personalized legal, tax, insurance or compliance advice for any client
exclusions: how indirect-reseller and partner (CSP-class) programs work, who bills whom, margin as a mechanism, support obligations to the program, anchor-suite choice, SMB segment selection, the trusted-IT-operator wedge, and ethical right-sizing of the license mix at the point of sale - that is the reseller-programs-and-targeting KB

monthly seat and license administration, true-ups, the ongoing support model and its boundaries, recurring security-posture reviews, renewal management, need-driven expansion paths and churn prevention - that is the subscription-management-and-expansion KB

quoting specific prices, per-seat rates, margins, setup fees or account multiples; commercial figures are treated as mechanisms whose current terms must be verified against the live partner program and the client's own quote
asserting specific statutory, regulatory or contractual requirements; obligation classes are named and current rules must be verified in the operator's jurisdiction
personalized legal, tax, insurance or financial advice to a client, which belongs with the client's own professionals
fear-based promotion of licenses, tiers or add-ons the client does not need, and any recommendation not traceable to an observed finding in that client's own environment
accessing, reading, retaining or repurposing client mail or files beyond the documented authorization and the least-privilege scope a specific task requires
enterprise-scale identity engineering (directory federation, elaborate conditional-access architectures) and full endpoint-management build-outs beyond the small-business baseline

competency_questions.question: Before touching a client's mail system, what authorization, access model and data-handling limits must exist, and how are they recorded?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ENGAGEMENT_AUTHORIZATION names the authorizing officer, approved requesters, in-scope systems and the revocable delegated-access model, and LEAST_PRIVILEGE_DATA_HANDLING states the per-task role scoping, credential lifecycle and content-access rule

competency_questions.question: What has to be inventoried in the client's current environment before a migration can be scoped, scheduled or promised?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SOURCE_ENVIRONMENT_DISCOVERY specifies the mailbox census with sizes and types, the permission map, aliases and lists, every device and application that sends as the domain, client devices, file locations and credential holders, gathered from consoles rather than memory

competency_questions.question: Who actually controls the domain and its DNS, and what must be proven about that control before a cutover date is promised?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DOMAIN_AND_DNS_CONTROL gives the registrant, registrar and DNS-host custody check, the zone export with per-record ownership, the proven test change, the TTL reduction plan, and the recovery path when a third party holds the domain

competency_questions.question: How is the tenant and its identity model laid out so that the decisions which cannot be reversed later are made correctly the first time?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TENANT_AND_IDENTITY_ARCHITECTURE separates creation-time fixed choices from changeable ones and defines UPN alignment, per-human accounts versus shared and resource mailboxes, group-driven membership and licensing, the naming standard, and the cloud-only versus directory-sync decision

competency_questions.question: What security baseline ships with every tenant, and how are administrative identities separated and multi-factor enforced without locking anyone - including the client - out?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ADMIN_SEPARATION_AND_BREAKGLASS defines separate admin identities, the client-held credential and the alerted break-glass account, MFA_ENFORCEMENT_BASELINE gives the method choice, enrolment order, enforcement date, legacy-authentication closure and exception register, and TENANT_SECURITY_BASELINE lists the repeatable hardening set with its deviation register

competency_questions.question: If a user, an administrator or an attacker deletes something, what is actually recoverable, from where, and for how long?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BACKUP_AND_RETENTION_DESIGN maps each loss scenario to a native or add-on recovery path with an owner and a time limit, states the deleted-account data window as a vendor-verified mechanism, and produces a recoverability statement the client has acknowledged

competency_questions.question: How is mail authentication and device or application mail flow designed so the domain keeps delivering after cutover and cannot be trivially spoofed?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MAIL_AUTHENTICATION_AND_FLOW consolidates authorization for every enumerated sender, enables and publishes signing, ramps policy from monitoring first, and assigns a relay or authentication method to each device and application

competency_questions.question: How is the migration method chosen, and what data actually moves at what fidelity?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MIGRATION_METHOD_SELECTION scores the candidate method families against source capability, volume, measured throughput and interruption tolerance and records the decision, and DATA_SCOPE_AND_FIDELITY gives the per-data-class in-or-out decision, the fidelity note and the manual rebuild list

competency_questions.question: How do shared files and collaboration data move without breaking permissions or drowning the client's laptops and connection in sync traffic?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FILE_AND_COLLABORATION_MIGRATION defines the shared-versus-personal destination layout, permission mapping onto groups, path and character remediation, the archive-versus-migrate decision, selective sync rollout and the count-and-access reconciliation

competency_questions.question: How is the cutover sequenced, rehearsed and verified so the business does not lose mail?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PILOT_MIGRATION measures real throughput and fidelity on a representative cohort, CUTOVER_RUNBOOK sets the timed sequence with owners, business-calendar constraints and a point of no return, and CUTOVER_EXECUTION_VERIFY proves delivery by two-way test per user, per shared mailbox and per sending device

competency_questions.question: What is the way back if the cutover goes wrong, and when is the old system finally safe to switch off?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ROLLBACK_AND_COEXISTENCE classifies what is reversible and what is not, defines the read-only source retention period and its access path, and gates decommission on acceptance, reconciliation, a client-held export and written approval

competency_questions.question: How are the client's people prepared, set up, taught and supported through the change so the switch does not become a ticket flood?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: USER_CHANGE_COMMUNICATION defines the message cadence, per-user action list and client-side sender, USER_ONBOARDING_TRAINING defines the per-user setup checklist and the narrow high-frequency curriculum, and HYPERCARE_TRIAGE defines the issue taxonomy, impact-first triage and the stated window with an explicit end

competency_questions.question: Onboarding always exposes security and licensing gaps - how are they raised without fear-selling licenses the client does not need?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SCOPE_DISCIPLINE_NO_FEAR_UPSELL requires a neutral findings register tied to observed evidence and materiality, a plain statement of what the current subscription already includes, a split between fixes that block safe delivery and matters for the scheduled review, and recorded declines

competency_questions.question: What documentation must exist at handover, and what acceptance gate ends the project and starts the recurring relationship?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: AS_BUILT_DOCUMENTATION lists the delivered-environment pack including credential custody and record ownership held by the client, and HANDOVER_ACCEPTANCE states the dated acceptance conditions, the proven client credential, the decommission decision and the project-to-service boundary

glossary.definition: The client's own isolated instance of the cloud suite - its identities, mailboxes, groups, files and policy settings. It belongs to the client even when a reseller administers it, and a number of its attributes are fixed at creation and can only be changed by building a new one.

An access model in which the client grants a partner administrative rights over their tenant through the vendor's partner relationship rather than by handing over a password; current partner (CSP-class) programs scope those rights by role and duration and let the client revoke them. The mechanism and its naming change between vendor programs and must be verified against the current program documentation.

A rarely used emergency administrator account held by the client, deliberately excluded from the policies that could block its sign-in, kept out of daily use and alerted on, so that a policy mistake, a lost second factor or a dispute with the supplier can never lock a business out of its own tenant.

The moment inbound delivery is redirected from the old system to the new one by changing the domain's mail-exchange records; because resolvers cache records for the length of the record's time-to-live, mail may arrive at both systems until the previous value expires everywhere.

The mechanism by which a mail client finds the correct server settings for an address, typically through specific DNS records or a vendor endpoint. When it still points at the old system, clients keep reconnecting to the wrong place after a cutover even though delivery itself is correct.

SPF publishes which systems may send for a domain, DKIM signs outbound mail so a receiver can verify it, and DMARC tells receivers what to do when neither passes while reporting who is sending as the domain. All three live in DNS and are only as good as the sender inventory behind them.

A transitional state in which both the old and the new system can still receive or hold mail for the domain, used to move users in waves or to keep a retrieval path open after cutover. It is deliberately temporary, because a split estate fragments threads and confuses users.

How faithfully each data class survives the move - mail, folder structure, calendars, contacts, delegate and send-as permissions, rules, categories and archives. Fidelity is a property of the chosen method and tool, so it cannot honestly be promised independently of them.

A mailbox for a role or function (an enquiries or accounts address) that several named people open with their own accounts and granted permissions, instead of everyone signing in to one generic account with one shared password. The distinction matters for security, for auditing and often for how the seat is licensed.

The explicitly time-boxed period straight after cutover in which the delivery team expects, triages and logs a wave of small issues. It has a stated start, end and scope precisely so that stabilization does not quietly become unlimited free support.

nodes.definition: Before any credential is issued or any record is changed, establish in writing who at the client may grant administrative access, what that access covers, and which named people may request changes to accounts and data. For a reseller this is a fiduciary-grade step rather than paperwork: a global-administrator credential in a business email tenant can read every director's mail, so the engagement must name the authorizing officer (usually the owner or a director), record the scope of systems, domains and mailboxes covered, list the approved requesters, and state the client's ownership of the tenant and its data from the first day. It also fixes the access model itself - delegated administration granted through the vendor's partner relationship and revocable by the client, rather than a personal password read out over the phone - together with the term of that access and how it ends.

included: named authorizing officer and approved-requester list
written scope of domains, systems and mailboxes covered
delegated, revocable access model rather than shared passwords
client ownership of the tenant and its data recorded from day one
the term of the access and how it is ended
excluded: partner-program enrolment and margin terms, which belong to the programs KB
the ongoing support scope and escalation ladder that follows handover
drafting the client's contracts, which is work for their own counsel

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an access dispute, or a request arriving that the existing authorization record does not clearly cover

pros.claim: A named authorizing officer plus an approved-requester list turns a request to open somebody else's mailbox from a judgement call into a documented procedure
pros.example: a manager phones asking for a departed colleague's mail to be forwarded to him; the request is routed to the authorizing officer and the written approval is filed with the change

pros.claim: Recording client ownership and a revocable access model at the start removes the lock-in suspicion that poisons reseller relationships later
pros.example: the owner can see in the engagement record exactly how to revoke the reseller's delegated access without losing their own tenant

cons.claim: Insisting on written authorization slows the first hours of an engagement and can read as bureaucratic to a ten-person firm that just wants its email fixed
cons.example: an owner who wants work started on a Friday afternoon has to be walked through a scope and access record before a single mailbox is touched

failure_modes: starting work on a verbal go-ahead and having no record when an access decision is later disputed
accepting the owner's personal password instead of establishing a delegated, revocable relationship
leaving the reseller as the only party holding tenant ownership, which is both a continuity risk and a commercial trap for the client
acceptance_tests: an authorization record exists naming the authorizing officer, the approved requesters, the in-scope domains and systems, and the access model, dated before the first administrative action
the client can state where tenant ownership sits and how to revoke the reseller's access without external help
revisit_triggers: the authorizing officer or an approved requester leaves the client
the engagement expands to a new domain, entity or system not named in the record

nodes.definition: Govern how client mail and files are actually touched during the project: which administrative role is used for which task, how migration service accounts and application consents are created and revoked, where staged data such as exported archive files or migration-tool copies lives, how it is encrypted and destroyed, and what content a technician may open at all. The working principle is that access is taken at the narrowest role that completes the task and for the shortest time - a migration account with mailbox-move rights rather than standing global administration, an export drive that is encrypted and wiped after acceptance, and a rule that mailbox content is opened only to reproduce a specific reported fault, with that access logged. The unit equally defines what the reseller never does: read, retain, index or repurpose client mail, or move client data through a personal account or an undisclosed third-party tool.

included: role selection per task with time-boxing
migration service-account and application-consent lifecycle including revocation
encryption and recorded destruction of staged exports
the content-access rule and its logging
disclosure to the client of every tool that touches their data
excluded: naming specific statutory data-protection duties, which vary and must be verified in your jurisdiction
the client's own internal data-retention policy decisions
ongoing alert monitoring and access review after handover, which is recurring-service work

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a security incident, a client access audit, or a change in a migration tool's access model

pros.claim: Task-scoped, time-boxed roles mean a compromised migration tool or a technician's mistake cannot reach the whole tenant
pros.example: the migration application's consent is revoked the day the final delta pass finishes rather than sitting in the tenant for years

pros.claim: A written content-access rule protects both sides when a client later asks what the reseller could see
pros.example: a logged, single-mailbox access to reproduce a reported missing-folder fault, with the reason recorded against the ticket

cons.claim: Least privilege slows troubleshooting, because the technician who needs to inspect a delegate permission has to escalate a role rather than already holding it
cons.example: a permissions fault takes an extra hour on a cutover night because the standing role was deliberately not global administrator

failure_modes: exported archive files left unencrypted on a technician's laptop or in a personal cloud account
migration service accounts and application consents that are never revoked after the project ends
opening a mailbox out of curiosity, which no log will excuse and no client will forgive
acceptance_tests: every credential, service account and application consent created for the migration appears on a register with an owner and a revocation date, and each is revoked or explicitly renewed at acceptance
staged exports are encrypted, their location is recorded, and their destruction after acceptance is evidenced
revisit_triggers: a new migration tool or sub-processor is introduced mid-project
a content-access request arrives that the authorization record does not cover

nodes.definition: Build the inventory every later decision rests on. That means the mail platform in use and its plan or version, the mailbox census with per-mailbox size and item count, which mailboxes are real humans and which are shared, role or resource addresses, aliases and distribution lists, delegate and send-as permissions, server-side rules and external forwards, archives and desktop archive files that users treat as their real filing system, where documents actually live (a file server, a sync service, personal drives), every device and application that sends mail as the domain from the copier to the invoicing package to the appointment-reminder service, the mail clients and mobile devices staff use, and who holds each relevant credential. The inventory is taken from admin consoles and exports rather than from what the owner remembers, because the gap between the two is precisely where migration failures live.

included: mailbox census with size, item count and mailbox type
permission, delegate, alias and distribution-list map
every device and application that sends as the domain, with an owner for each
client devices, mail clients and mobile estate
file-storage locations and desktop archive files
credential holders for each source system
excluded: pricing the engagement and choosing the license mix, which belong to the programs KB
tracking the same inventory as it drifts after handover, which is recurring-service work
the migration method itself, which this inventory feeds

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a post-cutover incident traced to an item that was absent from the inventory

pros.claim: A console export of mailbox sizes and item counts turns a guess about the migration window into an estimate the client can plan a working week around
pros.example: discovering that two of twelve mailboxes hold most of the data changes the wave plan before any date is promised

pros.claim: Asking what else sends mail as the domain surfaces the systems that fail silently after cutover
pros.example: the accounts package that emails invoices through an old relay is found during discovery instead of when a customer says the invoice never arrived

cons.claim: Thorough discovery costs unbilled hours before the client has committed, and some environments only reveal their surprises under migration load
cons.example: an undocumented appointment-reminder integration that only becomes visible when reminders stop going out after cutover

failure_modes: counting employees instead of mailboxes and missing every shared and resource mailbox
trusting the owner's headcount over the source console export
never asking what else sends mail as the domain, which guarantees a post-cutover surprise
acceptance_tests: a mailbox census exists with per-mailbox size, item count and type, reconciled against the source console rather than against headcount
a list of every device and application that sends as the domain exists, each with a named owner and its current sending method
revisit_triggers: a mailbox, alias or sending application appears that is not on the inventory
the client acquires, merges or spins out an entity mid-project

nodes.definition: Establish, before any date is promised, that the client can genuinely control the DNS zone their email depends on: who is the registrant of record, who holds the registrar login, whether DNS is served at the registrar or delegated to a web host or another provider, whether registrar lock and auto-renew are on, when the registration expires, and how fast a change can actually be applied by whoever holds that console. The unit includes exporting the current zone and labelling every record keep, change or retire, identifying the records that must not be disturbed such as a website address record or a third-party verification entry, lowering the time-to-live on the records that will change far enough ahead of the window, and resolving the ordinary small-business situation in which a former web developer or a dissolved agency still holds the domain. Without proven control there is no cutover date, only an aspiration.

included: registrant, registrar and DNS-host custody check
zone export with each record labelled keep, change or retire and an owner named
a proven test change by the party who will perform the cutover
time-to-live reduction planned ahead of the window
expiry, lock and auto-renew check, and the recovery path when a third party holds control
excluded: choosing or rebranding the domain name
website hosting and site content beyond the records mail depends on
routine DNS changes after handover, which are recurring-service work

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a failed or delayed record change, or a registrar or hosting change on the client side

pros.claim: Proving DNS control in the first week converts the riskiest external dependency into a scheduled task instead of a cutover-night discovery
pros.example: finding immediately that a former web developer holds the registrar login, so recovery starts weeks before any date is offered

pros.claim: A labelled zone export stops the cutover from collaterally breaking things that share the domain
pros.example: the record that verifies the client's payment provider is marked keep and survives the mail changes untouched

cons.claim: The recovery path when a third party holds the domain can take weeks and sits outside the reseller's control, stalling an otherwise ready project
cons.example: waiting on a registrar transfer while the client's staff ask daily when the new email starts

failure_modes: promising a cutover date before confirming who can change the mail records
letting a web host overwrite the zone during an unrelated website change
leaving the time-to-live reduction until the day of the cutover, so the old value still governs caches
acceptance_tests: a zone export exists with every record labelled keep, change or retire and the console that serves it named with its holder
a test record has been added and removed successfully by the party who will perform the cutover, and time-to-live values on the records to be changed have been lowered ahead of the window
revisit_triggers: the client changes registrar, web host or web developer
a record in the zone changes without a matching change record

nodes.definition: Lay out the tenant and its identity model in the order that respects what cannot be undone. Some tenant attributes are fixed when the tenant is created and can only be changed by building a new one, so the initial name, the region or data-location class and the primary domain are chosen knowingly and checked against the vendor's current documentation rather than assumed. The client's real domain is verified and made primary before the first account exists, so that sign-in names match the addresses people actually hand out. The account model then settles: one licensed account per human, role addresses as shared mailboxes rather than generic logins shared by three people, rooms and equipment as resource accounts, groups that drive both membership and license assignment, and a naming standard that will still read sensibly at three times the headcount. Finally the identity source is decided deliberately - for most small businesses cloud-only is simpler and cheaper than synchronizing an ageing on-premises directory, and that decision should be made rather than inherited.

included: creation-time choices that cannot be changed later, verified against current vendor documentation
domain verification and sign-in-name alignment with the primary address
per-human accounts, shared mailboxes for roles, resource accounts for rooms and equipment
group-driven membership and license assignment
naming standard for users, groups and shared mailboxes
the cloud-only versus directory-synchronized decision
excluded: which license SKUs are bought and what they cost or earn, which belongs to the programs KB
ongoing seat administration and true-ups after handover
the security policies layered on top of this model

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a rename, domain addition or restructure the current model cannot absorb without rework

pros.claim: Settling sign-in names and the naming standard before the first account exists prevents a rename campaign that would break logins, permissions and every saved profile
pros.example: catching that the client wants first-name addresses before fifteen accounts have been created in an initial-plus-surname pattern

pros.claim: Group-driven membership and licensing makes later joiner and leaver work a single action instead of a checklist nobody follows
pros.example: a new bookkeeper joins one group and receives the licence, the shared mailbox access and the finance library in one step

cons.claim: A clean model collides with entrenched habits, and imposing it during a migration adds change the users did not ask for
cons.example: converting a generic office login used by three staff into a shared mailbox forces three personal accounts and new habits at the worst possible moment

failure_modes: creating accounts before the client's domain is verified, so every sign-in name carries the vendor's default domain
replicating shared logins because the client asked for them, which destroys auditability from day one
no naming standard, so groups and shared mailboxes become unreadable within a year
acceptance_tests: the client's domain is verified and primary before the first user account is created, and every account's sign-in name matches its primary address
a written account model lists each human account, shared mailbox, resource account and group with its purpose, its members and its naming pattern
revisit_triggers: the client adds a second trading domain or a new legal entity
headcount or structure changes enough that the group and naming model no longer sorts cleanly

nodes.definition: Separate administrative power from daily work, and make sure nobody - including the reseller - can lock the client out of their own tenant. Day-to-day mailboxes do not carry global administrative rights; administrative work is done from a distinct account; the reseller works through a delegated relationship the client can revoke; and the client always holds at least one global-administrator credential of their own, stored where the owner can reach it without the reseller. A break-glass account is created with a long unique credential, excluded from the enforcement policies that could block it, kept out of daily use and alerted on so that any sign-in raises a flag. The reasoning is blunt: the accounts with the most power are exactly the ones attackers pursue, and a reseller holding the only administrative credential is a single point of failure the client never knowingly agreed to.

included: a separate administrative identity per administrator, distinct from their mailbox account
at least one client-held global-administrator credential and its custody arrangement
break-glass account creation, policy exclusion, storage and sign-in alerting
delegated reseller access that is scoped, time-bound and revocable
role assignment by least privilege rather than by convenience
excluded: the multi-factor method and enforcement mechanics, which are their own unit
periodic privileged-access reviews on the recurring cadence after handover
the client's internal decision about who should be an administrator

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a lockout event, a vendor change to delegated administration, or an administrator change on either side

pros.claim: A client-held administrative credential plus an alerted break-glass account means neither a compromised supplier nor a lost phone can strand the business
pros.example: the owner can still reach the tenant on a Sunday when the reseller's own account is suspended during an incident

pros.claim: Administering from an account that receives no mail removes the most common path from a phishing click to tenant-wide compromise
pros.example: a phishing message lands in the technician's ordinary mailbox, which holds no administrative rights at all

cons.claim: Extra administrative identities and an emergency account are more credentials to secure, and an unmonitored break-glass account is itself a liability
cons.example: a break-glass credential ends up on a note under the owner's keyboard because nobody agreed where it should live

failure_modes: the reseller holding the only global-administrator credential, which is simultaneously a lock-in and a continuity risk
creating a break-glass account and never configuring an alert on its use
administering the tenant from the same account that reads mail and clicks links
acceptance_tests: at least one global-administrator credential is held by a named client officer and the reseller's access is delegated and demonstrably revocable
a break-glass account exists, is excluded from the policies that could block sign-in, is absent from daily use, and raises an alert to a monitored destination when used
revisit_triggers: an administrator joins or leaves either the client or the reseller
the vendor changes how delegated administration or role assignment works

nodes.definition: Take the tenant from multi-factor being available to multi-factor being enforced with the legacy sign-in paths closed, in a sequence that locks nobody out mid-project. The work is: choose a method the client's staff can realistically use, favouring an authenticator application or a hardware key over text messages and documenting a fallback for the one employee without a suitable phone; enrol administrators first; run a registration window with an enforcement date the users have been told about in advance; block or tightly scope the older authentication protocols that bypass a second factor; and verify enforcement afterwards from sign-in data rather than assuming the switch worked. Because vendors keep changing defaults, enforcement surfaces and which protocols are being retired, the current mechanism must be checked against the vendor's live documentation for the client's plan at build time instead of from memory.

included: method selection with a documented fallback for users without a suitable phone
administrator-first enrolment order and a dated registration window
closure or scoping of legacy authentication paths
an exception register with owner, reason and expiry for each entry
post-enforcement verification from sign-in data
excluded: advanced conditional-access design that requires a higher licensing tier, which is a scheduled-review decision and must never be fear-sold during a cutover
the client's password policy for systems outside the tenant
identity-provider federation, which is outside the small-business baseline

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: vendor documentation showing a changed enforcement mechanism or a retired protocol, or a lockout or bypass incident in a delivered tenant

pros.claim: Enforcing at the tenant with a scheduled registration window turns multi-factor from an argument with each user into a dated project step
pros.example: administrators enrol in week one, staff enrol during the pilot, and enforcement flips on the announced date with the exception register already agreed

pros.claim: Closing the legacy authentication paths removes the bypass that makes enforcement cosmetic
pros.example: sign-in data after the enforcement date shows no successful legacy protocol sign-ins for in-scope accounts

cons.claim: Enforcement breaks everything that authenticated with a stored password - old handsets, scanners and small applications - and those breakages are reported as the new email being broken
cons.example: a warehouse tablet running an old mail client stops sending the morning stock report the night enforcement is switched on

failure_modes: enabling enforcement before the break-glass exclusion exists, so a policy error locks out the tenant
granting a permanent exception to the owner, who is the most targeted account in the business
assuming legacy protocols are off because the vendor announced a retirement, without checking this tenant
acceptance_tests: every enabled account either has a registered second factor or an entry in the exception register carrying an owner, a reason and an expiry date
sign-in data after the enforcement date shows no successful legacy-authentication sign-ins for in-scope accounts, and the break-glass exclusion is confirmed still in place
revisit_triggers: the vendor changes enforcement defaults or retires an authentication path
an exception passes its expiry date, or a lockout is reported

nodes.definition: The written, repeatable set of tenant settings applied to every client so that a secure default is a product rather than an act of memory: anti-phishing and anti-spam handling including impersonation protection for the owner and the finance addresses, external-sender marking, restriction of automatic forwarding to outside addresses, mailbox audit logging switched on, calendar and file sharing defaults set deliberately instead of left wide, alerting on suspicious sign-ins and on new inbox rules routed to an address a human actually reads, and limits on users granting third-party applications access to their mailbox. Each deviation for a particular client is written down with a reason, an owner and a date. The baseline is expressed as capability classes rather than as exact toggle names because those names, their locations and their defaults differ between vendors, plans and releases and must be re-checked against current vendor documentation whenever the baseline is applied.

included: the standard hardening set stated as capability classes
per-client deviation register with reason, owner and date
alert destinations and the named human who reads them
third-party application consent limits and external sharing defaults
recording which baseline version was applied to this tenant
excluded: paid add-on security tooling and the decision to buy it, which is a scheduled-review matter and never a cutover-day upsell
endpoint and device management, which is an expansion path in the recurring KB
incident response after handover

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a vendor default change, a new capability class, or an incident revealing a gap the baseline did not cover

pros.claim: One baseline applied to every tenant makes the delivered environment predictable, checkable and quick to hand to a second technician
pros.example: any client tenant can be walked against the same list, so a missing audit setting is a five-minute find rather than an archaeology exercise

pros.claim: Restricting automatic external forwarding closes the quiet exfiltration path that follows most mailbox compromises
pros.example: an attacker who obtains a password cannot silently copy the finance mailbox to an outside address without tripping the restriction

cons.claim: A fixed baseline collides with real workflows that depend on the very things it restricts, and every exception erodes the standard
cons.example: a bookkeeper's automatic forward to an external accountant breaks, and the exception has to be scoped, justified and recorded rather than simply granted

failure_modes: applying settings from memory, so every tenant differs subtly and none can be audited
granting silent exceptions under cutover pressure that are never recorded
routing alerts to an address nobody reads, which is worse than not alerting at all
acceptance_tests: the tenant has been walked item by item against the written baseline and every deviation is recorded with a reason, an owner and a date
a test alert reaches its monitored destination and the person who receives it can say what they would do with it
revisit_triggers: the vendor changes a default or introduces a new capability class within the baseline's scope
an incident or near miss shows the baseline missed a whole class of risk

nodes.definition: Decide and write down what can actually be recovered, from where and for how long, before the client needs it. The suite's own recycle bins, retention settings and hold features cover some loss classes and not others, their windows differ by plan and change over time, and data belonging to a deleted account in particular disappears on a vendor-defined schedule that has to be checked rather than assumed. The unit enumerates the loss scenarios this client is genuinely exposed to - a user emptying a folder and the bin, an account deleted at offboarding, ransomware encrypting synchronized files, a compromised mailbox wiped by an intruder - maps each to a native capability or to an add-on, judges whether a third-party backup is warranted by that exposure rather than by sales pressure, and defines how a restore would actually be performed and by whom. The output is a recoverability statement the client has read and acknowledged, replacing the assumption that anything in the cloud is automatically backed up.

included: enumerated loss scenarios mapped to a native or add-on recovery path
the deleted-account data window as a vendor-verified mechanism, plus the export step in offboarding
retention and hold settings applied to this tenant
a restore procedure with a named owner and a proven test restore
a plain statement of what is not recoverable at all
excluded: quoting backup product prices or margins, which are commercial matters for the other KBs
promoting a backup add-on on fear rather than an identified exposure
the ongoing restore-test cadence, which is a recurring-service commitment

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a real restore attempt that succeeded or failed, or a vendor change to a retention window or plan capability

pros.claim: A written recoverability statement replaces a dangerous assumption with a decision the client actually made and can be held to
pros.example: the client reads that an offboarded account's data disappears on a vendor schedule and agrees to add a mailbox export step to the leaver checklist

pros.claim: Testing one real restore during the project proves the recovery path exists rather than merely describing it
pros.example: a deliberately deleted test document is recovered end to end and the steps are captured in the documentation pack

cons.claim: Backup adds a recurring cost the smallest clients resent until the day they need it, and honest framing sometimes means recommending no add-on at all
cons.example: a four-person firm with little unique file data is told the native features plus an export step are proportionate, which forgoes an add-on sale

failure_modes: assuming the vendor keeps everything indefinitely because it is in the cloud
deleting an offboarded account before its data has been exported and its window has been checked
protecting mail while leaving the collaboration files that the same business depends on uncovered
acceptance_tests: each identified loss scenario has a named recovery path, an owner and a stated time limit, and the client has acknowledged the recoverability statement in writing
at least one restore has been performed successfully in the delivered tenant rather than only described
revisit_triggers: the vendor changes a retention window or what a plan includes
the client's data profile changes materially, for instance by taking on records with a longer obligation class

nodes.definition: Design the domain's sending story so that mail still arrives after the cutover and cannot be trivially forged. Every system that sends as the domain - the new tenant, the website contact form, the customer-relationship tool, the invoicing package, the marketing platform, the copier that emails scans, the appointment-reminder service - is enumerated from discovery and then either authorized in a single consolidated sender-authorization record, moved to a subdomain of its own, or re-pointed to authenticate through the tenant. Outbound signing is enabled and published for the domain, and reporting policy is introduced in monitoring mode first so the reports reveal who is genuinely sending before anything is tightened toward quarantine or rejection. Sequence is the whole discipline here: publishing a strict policy before the sender inventory is complete silently kills legitimate mail from the systems nobody remembered.

included: a single consolidated authorization record covering every enumerated sender, within the protocol's lookup limits
outbound signing enabled and published
monitor-first policy ramp with report review before any tightening
a relay or authentication method assigned to each device and application
subdomain strategy for bulk or third-party senders
excluded: marketing deliverability strategy and list hygiene
website hosting records beyond those mail depends on
ongoing report monitoring after handover, which is recurring-service work

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: aggregate reports revealing unknown senders, or a delivery failure traced to authentication

pros.claim: A monitor-first ramp reveals the forgotten senders while a policy change can still be adjusted rather than after it has bounced them
pros.example: reports show the accounting package still sending as the domain through a provider nobody listed, caught weeks before any enforcement

pros.claim: Consolidating authorization into one valid record removes the silent invalidation that multiple or over-long records cause
pros.example: two competing authorization records left by a previous supplier are merged into one that resolves within the lookup limit

cons.claim: The full ramp takes weeks of report reading that a fixed setup fee does not obviously pay for, and tightening early causes exactly the outage it was meant to prevent
cons.example: a client who wants everything finished this week pressing for a strict policy on day two, before the inventory is closed

failure_modes: leaving multiple authorization records, or a lookup chain too long to evaluate, so nothing is actually authorized
moving to a strict policy before the sender inventory is complete
leaving the copier relaying unauthenticated and discovering it only when scans stop arriving
acceptance_tests: a single valid authorization record covers every enumerated sender and resolves within the protocol's lookup limits, and outbound signing verifies on a test message from the tenant
policy has run in monitoring mode long enough for reports to show only known senders before any tightening is proposed
revisit_triggers: a new application or device begins sending as the domain
reports show an unrecognized source or an authentication failure rate above the agreed threshold

nodes.definition: Choose how the data actually moves, given what the source platform supports and how much interruption this business can absorb. The families are: a single-event cutover in which everything moves and the records switch in one window, which is cheapest and fits small mailbox counts; a staged or wave migration in which users move in batches with coexistence in between, which becomes necessary as volume or seat count outgrows a single window; a longer coexistence arrangement in which both systems deliver during a transition, which is the heaviest to build and is justified only for larger or highly interruption-sensitive clients; and file-level or protocol-level transfer using export and import or a third-party migration tool where no native path exists. Each candidate is scored against source-platform capability, total volume and per-mailbox size, throughput measured in the pilot, the fidelity it preserves, the freeze the client can tolerate, and what it costs to build. The chosen path is written down with its reasoning, because it determines the runbook, the communication and the rollback position that follow.

included: candidate method families and the prerequisites each imposes
volume, throughput and window sizing
the client's interruption tolerance as an explicit input
tool selection and the access model that tool requires
the written decision with its reasoning
excluded: the fidelity of individual data classes, decided in its own unit
executing the cutover itself
how the setup fee is quoted, which belongs to the programs KB

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: measured pilot throughput, or a source-platform capability change that invalidates the chosen path

pros.claim: Matching method to volume and interruption tolerance avoids both the over-engineered coexistence build and the weekend cutover that runs into Tuesday
pros.example: a firm whose two largest mailboxes dominate the data is moved in waves so the ten small mailboxes are live on Monday morning

pros.claim: Writing the decision down keeps the runbook, the client communication and the rollback position consistent with one another
pros.example: the recorded choice of a wave migration explains why the records change only after the final wave rather than on night one

cons.claim: The method has to be chosen before throughput is truly known, and source platforms impose limits that only appear under load
cons.example: a source provider that throttles concurrent connections turns a one-night plan into three nights

failure_modes: choosing a single-event cutover because it is cheapest, without checking that the volume fits the window
selecting a migration tool whose access model the tenant's own security baseline forbids
not recording why the method was chosen, so the runbook quietly contradicts it
acceptance_tests: the selected method is recorded together with the source-platform capability, the volume, the estimated or measured throughput and the interruption tolerance it was chosen against
the source and destination access the chosen tool needs has been proven on a real account before any window is scheduled
revisit_triggers: pilot throughput differs materially from the planning estimate
the source platform changes its export capability or imposes new limits

nodes.definition: Decide in writing, with the client, exactly which data classes move and how faithfully each will arrive, because the gap between we moved your email and what a user finds on Monday morning is the most common source of migration disputes. Mail and folder structure, calendars, contacts, shared mailboxes, distribution lists, room bookings, delegate and send-as permissions, server-side rules, categories, signatures, archives and desktop archive files, and everything older than a chosen archive date each need an explicit in-or-out decision and an honest fidelity note: some methods carry folders but not rules, some carry mail but not calendar sharing, and permission and delegation maps very often have to be rebuilt by hand at the destination. The output is a short fidelity statement the client acknowledges, the users are told about in advance, and a manual rebuild list with an owner for everything the tool cannot carry.

included: a per-data-class in-or-out decision
a fidelity note per class and the resulting manual rebuild list with owners
the archive cut-off decision and how older material is preserved
desktop archive file discovery and handling
the client-facing statement of what will not move
excluded: the transfer mechanism itself
file-share and collaboration content, handled in its own unit
retention policy design at the destination, handled in the recoverability unit

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a post-cutover complaint about data the client assumed was in scope, or a change of migration method

pros.claim: An acknowledged fidelity statement converts Monday-morning surprises into expectations that were set weeks earlier
pros.example: users are told in advance that client-side rules must be recreated, and a short how-to is included in the training pack

pros.claim: A manual rebuild list with owners gets delegate and send-as permissions restored inside the window instead of during the first busy morning
pros.example: the two directors' assistants have their delegate access rebuilt and tested before the office opens

cons.claim: Every honest exclusion invites a negotiation that can expand scope, and some clients read the fidelity note as evidence the supplier is not competent
cons.example: a client insisting that fifteen years of nested folders and every rule must arrive identically, which changes both method and price

failure_modes: promising that everything moves because it sounds better than the truth
missing desktop archive files that users consider their real filing system
having no manual rebuild list, so missing delegate permissions are discovered by the people who need them most
acceptance_tests: every data class carries a documented in-or-out decision and a fidelity note, and the client has acknowledged the statement of what will not move
the manual rebuild list exists with an owner per item and is scheduled inside the cutover plan rather than left to goodwill
revisit_triggers: a data class nobody scoped, such as a desktop archive or a shared calendar, is discovered
the migration method changes, since fidelity is a property of the method

nodes.definition: Move the shared files as deliberately as the mail, because a file server or a sprawl of personal drives is where small-business collaboration actually lives. The work covers deciding what belongs in a team library versus each user's personal storage, mapping existing share permissions onto groups instead of recreating hundreds of individual grants, handling the mechanical hazards - paths that are too long, characters the destination rejects, files locked open by an application, enormous media archives, versions and checked-out documents - deciding what is archived rather than migrated, and rolling the sync client out with selective sync so no laptop is asked to pull down the entire estate over a small office connection. The judgement call is how much cleanup to do in flight: migration is the only moment a client will ever tolerate a conversation about their folder structure, and every hour spent restructuring is an hour the mail cutover does not get.

included: destination layout for shared versus personal content
permission mapping onto groups rather than individuals
path, character, lock and size remediation before transfer
the archive-versus-migrate decision for old material
sync client rollout with selective sync and bandwidth awareness
count, size and access reconciliation after transfer
excluded: mailbox data, handled elsewhere
records-management consulting beyond the destination layout
ongoing storage growth and add-on storage decisions after handover

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: reconciliation gaps, or user behaviour showing the old share is still in daily use

pros.claim: Mapping permissions onto groups during the move leaves the client with an access model they can maintain, instead of thousands of individual grants nobody dares touch
pros.example: the finance folder becomes a group-permissioned library, so a new bookkeeper gains access by joining one group

pros.claim: Selective sync decided up front protects the office connection and the laptops on the first morning
pros.example: the archive library is left online-only rather than pulled down onto every device at nine o'clock on Monday

cons.claim: File migrations expose years of accumulated mess, and the cleanup conversation can consume the schedule the mail cutover needs
cons.example: discovering three overlapping copies of the same project tree the week before the cutover window

failure_modes: syncing an entire large estate to every laptop and saturating the client's connection on the first morning
recreating per-user permissions one by one instead of mapping them onto groups
migrating while users keep editing the source, so the newest versions are the ones left behind
acceptance_tests: source and destination file counts and total size reconcile within an agreed tolerance, with every exception listed and explained
a sample of users can open, edit and save the files they need at the destination, and the sync client is configured not to pull unnecessary content
revisit_triggers: users keep saving into the old share after cutover
storage growth or sync complaints suggest the layout or the selective-sync choice was wrong

nodes.definition: Move a small, deliberately representative group before committing to the production window: the owner or the internal champion, one very large mailbox, one shared mailbox, one user with delegate permissions, and one user on the most awkward device in the building. The pilot is not a demonstration, it is the measurement that turns assumptions into numbers - real per-mailbox throughput, whether the migration tool's access model survives the security baseline that was just applied, whether permissions and calendars genuinely carry, how long a device and profile rebuild takes per person, and which support questions arrive first. Its outputs are a revised window estimate, a corrected fidelity note, an updated per-user setup script for the technician, and an explicit decision to proceed, to re-plan, or to change method.

included: representative cohort selection including a heavy, a shared and a delegated case
measured throughput and per-user setup time
fidelity verification against the acknowledged statement
an issue log whose fixes are folded back into the runbook
an explicit proceed, re-plan or change-method decision
excluded: the full production migration
the client's acceptance of the finished project
producing the training material, although the pilot informs it

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: pilot measurements that contradict the planning assumptions

pros.claim: A pilot turns a promised window from an estimate into a measured projection and surfaces the unglamorous blockers while there is still time to act
pros.example: learning that each device needs a profile rebuild taking far longer than assumed, which re-sizes the whole onboarding day

pros.claim: Piloting the awkward cases proves whether the security baseline and the migration tool can coexist before the whole business depends on it
pros.example: the tool's access request is rejected by the new tenant baseline during the pilot rather than at midnight on cutover night

cons.claim: The pilot consumes part of a fixed setup fee, and pilot users live in a split state where some mail is in the old system and some in the new
cons.example: a champion who has to check two places for a week and says so loudly if the reason was never explained

failure_modes: piloting only easy mailboxes, so the measurement flatters the plan
not folding pilot fixes back into the runbook, so the same problems recur at scale
letting the pilot drift into an indefinite half-migrated state with no decision
acceptance_tests: the pilot cohort includes at least one very large mailbox, one shared mailbox and one delegated-permission case, and measured throughput and per-user setup time are recorded
every pilot issue is either fixed in the runbook or explicitly accepted with a reason before the production window is scheduled
revisit_triggers: measured throughput or setup time diverges from the plan beyond the agreed tolerance
a fidelity gap appears that the acknowledged statement did not cover

nodes.definition: Write the cutover as a timed sequence with owners, checkpoints and a stated point of no return, then schedule it against the client's business calendar rather than the reseller's. The runbook names the pre-stage synchronization and its completion criterion, confirms the time-to-live reduction already applied, states the freeze instruction given to users, fixes the exact order of record changes, specifies the delta pass, lists the per-user device steps, sets the verification checks that must pass before the window can close, names who is on call and how the client reaches that person, and defines what would trigger a rollback. Scheduling is part of the plan, not an afterthought: payroll runs, month-end, a tax deadline, a seasonal peak, a trade show or the single day the bookkeeper is in all determine when a cutover must not happen. A runbook that lives only in the technician's head is not a plan - the test is whether a second person could execute it.

included: timed step sequence with owners, durations and pass criteria
pre-stage and delta-pass criteria
user freeze instruction and its duration
record-change order and the point of no return
business-calendar scheduling constraints confirmed in writing
on-call contact, escalation path and rollback trigger
excluded: execution and verification themselves
the content of user training
the recurring change-management process that applies after handover

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a cutover that deviated from its plan, or a scheduling conflict discovered too late

pros.claim: A written runbook lets a second technician run or finish the cutover and turns the rollback decision into a criterion rather than a panic
pros.example: the rule that records change only after the delta pass completes stops a well-meaning shortcut at midnight

pros.claim: Scheduling against the client's calendar prevents the outage that costs the most
pros.example: the window is moved off payroll week once the bookkeeper's cycle is checked with the authorizing officer

cons.claim: Building the runbook takes hours the client never sees, and an over-detailed plan can lull the operator into following steps instead of watching what is actually happening
cons.example: an evening spent planning a five-mailbox move that then runs in under an hour

failure_modes: scheduling the cutover onto payroll day, month-end or a seasonal peak
leaving no defined point of no return, so rollback becomes a judgement call under pressure
having no owner for the client-side communication step, so users learn about the change as it happens
acceptance_tests: the runbook lists each step with an owner, a duration and a pass criterion, and names both the point of no return and the rollback trigger
the scheduled window has been checked against the client's payroll, month-end and seasonal calendar and confirmed in writing by the authorizing officer
revisit_triggers: the business calendar changes or the window slips
a pilot finding or a method change alters the step sequence

nodes.definition: Prepare the client's people for a change to the tool they use most, on a schedule and in the client's own voice. The pack is small and concrete: what is changing and when, what each person must do and by when such as registering a second factor and knowing their new sign-in, what will look different on the first morning, what will not move and what to do about it, who to ask for help and how to reach them during the window, and a plain admission that the first days will produce small annoyances which get fixed quickly. It goes out on a cadence - an announcement, a reminder before the window, a note on the day and a note the morning after - signed by the owner or the internal champion rather than by an unfamiliar supplier address, because staff act on messages from their own management and ignore messages from vendors.

included: announcement, reminder, day-of and morning-after messages
a per-user action list with deadlines
the internal champion and the client-side signer of each message
the help route during and immediately after the window
honest expectation-setting about small disruptions
excluded: hands-on training content and its delivery
the ongoing support model and its response commitments
communication to the client's own customers, unless it was explicitly scoped

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: cutover-day ticket volume traceable to a message that was never sent or never read

pros.claim: Messages sent by the owner or champion actually get acted on, which is why second-factor registration completes before the window instead of during it
pros.example: a reminder from the owner two days out lifts enrolment from a handful of staff to nearly everyone

pros.claim: Naming a single help route stops every question landing on the owner's phone during the busiest hour
pros.example: staff are told to message the champion first, who batches the genuine faults to the technician

cons.claim: Communication is the first thing dropped when a project runs late, and over-communicating can create anxiety in a small office
cons.example: a detailed technical notice that leaves five staff convinced they are about to lose their email

failure_modes: sending nothing until the day of the cutover
writing in supplier jargon that staff cannot act on
naming no human to ask, so everyone calls the owner
acceptance_tests: the announcement, reminder and day-of messages have gone out from a client-side sender, and each names the required actions, the dates and the help route
second-factor registration and any other per-user prerequisite are confirmed complete before the window opens
revisit_triggers: the cutover date moves
prerequisite completion such as second-factor registration stalls below the agreed threshold

nodes.definition: Execute the runbook and then prove by test, not by tool report, that mail flows. Inside the window that means completing the delta pass, changing the records in the planned order, watching propagation from more than one vantage point rather than from the technician's own resolver, and then verifying: send and receive against an external address in both directions, test a reply to a message that was in flight during the switch, confirm that client auto-configuration points at the new service, re-point or re-authenticate the copier and every application relay, re-add mobile profiles, and check that each shared mailbox and each delegate permission genuinely opens for the person who needs it. Every check is ticked per user and per system rather than sampled in aggregate, because the migration reported success and the office manager can send from the shared address are entirely different claims.

included: delta pass completion and the ordered record change
propagation checks from multiple vantage points
two-way external mail tests including an in-flight reply
auto-configuration and profile verification
device and application relay re-point and test message
per-user and per-shared-mailbox verification ticks
excluded: the plan that ordered these steps
the training that follows
long-tail issue handling in the stabilization window

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a post-window delivery failure that the verification checklist should have caught

pros.claim: Per-user verification catches the one mailbox that silently failed, before its owner finds it on Monday
pros.example: a shared mailbox that migrated but whose send-as permission did not carry is found and fixed inside the window

pros.claim: Testing every sending device closes the failure class that nobody notices until a customer complains
pros.example: the copier delivers a test scan through its new authenticated path before the technician leaves the site

cons.claim: Verification lengthens the window and needs client-side participation at inconvenient hours, which small businesses resist
cons.example: asking the office manager to test the shared mailbox at nine on a Sunday evening

failure_modes: trusting the migration tool's success report instead of testing delivery
declaring the window closed before external mail has been tested in both directions
forgetting the devices and applications that send as the domain
acceptance_tests: external send and receive tests pass in both directions for a sampled set of users plus every shared mailbox, and each device or application that sends as the domain has delivered a test message after the change
every migrated user has an individually ticked verification line rather than an aggregate pass
revisit_triggers: any verification line fails or is skipped to save time
delivery complaints arrive in the days after the window

nodes.definition: Keep a way back, and decide deliberately when to give it up. Before the window, classify what is genuinely reversible - record changes can be reverted, subject to cache expiry - and what is not, such as a deleted source mailbox, a re-provisioned server or a cancelled source subscription. Keep the source system alive and reachable in a read-only or reduced state for a defined period after cutover so anything missed can still be retrieved, and where the method supports it arrange dual delivery or forwarding so nothing addressed to the old system is lost. The coexistence period then has an end: a decommission gate requiring acceptance, a completed reconciliation, an export of the source data held by the client, and written approval before the old system is cancelled or wiped. Cancelling the source subscription the day after cutover to save one month of fees is the classic way to turn a recoverable problem into a permanent loss.

included: reversible versus irreversible classification with time limits
the source read-only retention period and who can reach it
dual delivery or forwarding where the method supports it
the decommission gate and its conditions
custody of the final source export
excluded: the ongoing backup design for the new tenant
the client's contractual termination terms with the source provider
renewal administration of the new subscription

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a retrieval that failed because the source had already been decommissioned

pros.claim: A live read-only source turns a missing folder from an incident into a retrieval
pros.example: a user finds a two-year-old thread missing three weeks after cutover and it is pulled from the still-reachable source

pros.claim: A written decommission gate stops the irreversible step from being taken casually to save a month's subscription
pros.example: the old server is only wiped after acceptance, reconciliation and a client-held export are all evidenced

cons.claim: Keeping the old system paid and reachable costs money and lets users keep working in it, fragmenting mail across two systems
cons.example: a partner who never switched clients keeps replying from the old account, so half the thread is invisible to everyone else

failure_modes: cancelling the source subscription immediately to save a month's fee
setting no end to coexistence, so the client pays for two systems indefinitely
wiping a server before the client actually holds an export of what was on it
acceptance_tests: the rollback position is written down stating what is reversible, by whom and within what time, and the source remains reachable for the agreed period
the source is decommissioned only after acceptance, reconciliation, a client-held export and written approval, each evidenced
revisit_triggers: a retrieval request arrives near the end of the coexistence period
mail is observed still arriving into the source system

nodes.definition: Get every person working in the new environment and teach the handful of things that otherwise generate most of the support load. Per user that means the mail profile on desktop and mobile, second-factor enrolment confirmed rather than assumed, the signature restored, shared mailboxes and calendars visible, delegate access working, files reachable through the sync client, and scanning or printing to mail still functioning. The teaching is deliberately narrow: how to find mail by searching rather than by folder archaeology, how to send from a shared address, how to share a calendar, how to recover a deleted item, how to read the external-sender warning and what to do with a suspicious message, and where documents now live. It is delivered as short sessions or floor-walking rather than a lecture, leaves a one-page reference behind, and is aimed at the tasks this business actually performs rather than at a tour of features.

included: a per-user setup checklist covering desktop, mobile, shared access, files and scanning
confirmed second-factor enrolment per user
the narrow high-frequency curriculum
a one-page reference left with the client
the champion's role as the first person staff ask
excluded: ongoing user training as a recurring commercial service
training on applications unrelated to the suite
stabilization triage, which follows this unit

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the ticket mix in the first weeks showing which tasks the training failed to cover

pros.claim: Teaching five high-frequency tasks removes most of the tickets a migration would otherwise generate in its first month
pros.example: ten minutes on searching and on sending from the shared address prevents the two most common calls

pros.claim: A completed per-user checklist makes the exceptions visible by name instead of hiding them in an average
pros.example: the two field staff who were never set up appear as open lines rather than as a surprise the following week

cons.claim: Training time sits inside a fixed setup fee and scales with headcount, so it is the first thing squeezed when a project runs long
cons.example: a twenty-user client where the planned training day quietly shrinks to two hours of floor-walking

failure_modes: handing out a sign-in and calling it onboarding
training only the people who happen to be in the office, leaving part-time and field staff untouched
teaching features rather than the tasks these people actually do every day
acceptance_tests: every user has a completed setup checklist covering desktop, mobile, shared access and files, with exceptions listed by name and scheduled
the high-frequency task list has been demonstrated to each group and a one-page reference has been left with the client
revisit_triggers: the same question recurs repeatedly during the stabilization window
a group of users was missed, or new staff joined after the training

nodes.definition: Run a defined, time-boxed period after cutover in which issues are expected, triaged quickly and used as evidence. The predictable classes are a device still pointed at the old server, a cached credential prompting endlessly, a missing folder that turns out to be an unmigrated archive, a delegate or send-as permission that did not carry, a rule that no longer runs, a distribution list whose members were never recreated, an application that has quietly stopped sending, and a user who is still working in the old system. Each is triaged by business impact rather than by arrival order, with anything that stops mail flowing taking precedence over cosmetic complaints. The window has a stated start, a stated end and a stated scope, and closing it is a deliberate, communicated act that hands the account into the recurring support arrangement rather than a silent drift into unlimited free help.

included: the expected issue taxonomy with a first-response action per class
triage ordered by business impact, mail-flow failures first
a running issue log that feeds documentation and training updates
the stated window length and its communicated end
the handoff conversation into the recurring arrangement
excluded: the recurring support model, its response commitments and its pricing
permanent monitoring of the tenant
new work requested during the window, which is change rather than defect

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the issue log's composition and arrival curve across several completed migrations

pros.claim: A named window with a taxonomy makes the messy week after cutover a managed process instead of an open-ended obligation
pros.example: three permission faults and two device faults on day one are cleared in a morning because they were expected and already scripted

pros.claim: Logging every issue turns the first week into evidence that improves the next migration
pros.example: the recurring missing-archive class leads to an explicit archive question being added to the discovery inventory

cons.claim: Stabilization is intense unbilled work at exactly the moment the project fee is exhausted, and every quiet extension teaches the client to expect free support
cons.example: a window that slides from one week into a month because nobody ever said it had ended

failure_modes: never declaring the window closed, so migration support becomes permanent free support
handling issues in arrival order, so a whole-office mail-flow fault waits behind a signature request
fixing issues without recording them, which loses the evidence that should update the runbook
acceptance_tests: the window's start, end and scope were stated to the client in writing before cutover, and its closure was confirmed in writing afterwards
every logged issue carries a class, a resolution and a note on whether the runbook, the documentation or the training needs updating
revisit_triggers: the issue arrival rate is still rising as the window's stated end approaches
the same issue class recurs after the window has closed

nodes.definition: Handle the security and licensing gaps that discovery inevitably exposes in a way that serves the client rather than the invoice. Onboarding is the moment of greatest client anxiety and greatest information asymmetry - the reseller has just seen the mailbox with no second factor, the password three people share, the file share open to everyone - and that is exactly why fear framing works here and is therefore ruled out. The practice is to record every finding in a neutral register stating what was observed, what could follow from it and how material it is for this particular business; to say plainly which mitigations are already included in what the client pays for today; to split what must be fixed now because it blocks safe delivery from what is worth reviewing later; to recommend nothing that is not tied to an observed finding; and to defer non-urgent expansion to the scheduled review instead of closing it while the client is under cutover stress. When a client declines, the decline is recorded with its date and reason and the relationship carries on.

included: a neutral findings register tied to observed evidence with a materiality judgement
a plain statement of which mitigations the current subscription already includes
the split between fixes that block safe delivery and matters for the scheduled review
recorded declines with date and stated reason
deferral of non-urgent expansion to the scheduled review
excluded: the expansion catalogue, its pricing and the review cadence, which belong to the recurring KB
license-mix right-sizing at the point of sale, which belongs to the programs KB
anything amounting to personalized legal, insurance or financial advice, which belongs with the client's own professionals

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a client complaint about pressure selling, or a declined finding that later caused real harm

pros.claim: A neutral register with materiality lets the client make a real decision and makes the reseller's advice worth trusting for years
pros.example: recording that the owner's mailbox had no second factor, that it is high materiality, and that the fix is already included in the subscription they pay for rather than being an add-on

pros.claim: Recording declines stops the same recommendation being re-litigated annually and protects both sides if the risk later materializes
pros.example: a declined backup add-on is logged with the client's stated reason and revisited only when the business changes

cons.claim: Declining to fear-sell forgoes revenue a less scrupulous competitor will take, and some clients only act under pressure
cons.example: a client defers a warranted backup add-on precisely because it was presented as a considered option rather than an emergency

failure_modes: presenting a generic threat narrative instead of what was actually observed in this tenant
bundling an unneeded higher tier into the migration quote because the moment is commercially convenient
never recording declines, so the client feels pressured every year by the same conversation
acceptance_tests: every recommendation in the handover pack cites an observed finding in this client's own environment and states whether the mitigation is already included in the current subscription
