declined recommendations are recorded with a date and the client's stated reason, and no recommendation relies on a threat framing unsupported by an observed finding
revisit_triggers: a declined finding's materiality changes because the business changed
a finding class appears that the register does not yet describe

nodes.definition: Produce the document that describes the environment as actually delivered, in a form the client owns and a second technician could work from: the tenant identifier and sign-in domain, every domain with its records and the console that serves them and who holds that console, the account and group model with how licences are assigned, every shared and resource mailbox with who has access, the security baseline applied together with each recorded deviation, the mail authentication records and the list of authorized senders, the recoverability decisions and the restore path, third-party applications and the permissions they hold, the credential custody map showing what the client holds and what the reseller holds and how to revoke it, and the migration record with its fidelity statement. It is written as the environment is built rather than reconstructed from memory afterwards, and a copy lives with the client rather than only inside the reseller's own systems.

included: tenant, domains, records and console custody
account, group and licence-assignment model with shared and resource mailboxes
baseline applied and every deviation
mail authentication records and the authorized sender list
recoverability decisions and the restore path
third-party application permissions
credential custody and how to revoke each one
the migration record and its fidelity statement
excluded: the reseller's internal pricing, margin or partner-program detail
the running change log maintained after handover
the client's own internal policies and procedures

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a question during handover or later support that the pack failed to answer

pros.claim: An as-built pack held by the client removes the lock-in that makes clients resent their supplier, and lets a second technician answer a question without the original engineer
pros.example: a holiday-week records question is answered from the pack in minutes instead of waiting for the one person who remembers

pros.claim: Documenting credential custody, not just settings, gives the client the part they actually need in a crisis
pros.example: the owner can see exactly which credential they hold, where it is stored and how to revoke the reseller's access

cons.claim: Documentation is invisible to the client until the day they need it, and it decays the first time somebody makes a change without updating it
cons.example: a record changed during an urgent fix that the pack never reflects, so the next technician works from a false map

failure_modes: writing it at the end from memory, so it is wrong in exactly the details that matter
keeping it only inside the reseller's systems, which quietly recreates lock-in
documenting settings while omitting credential custody
acceptance_tests: the pack covers tenant, domains and records with console custody, the account and group model, the baseline and its deviations, mail authentication and authorized senders, recoverability and restore, third-party application permissions, and credential custody, and the client holds their own copy
a technician who did not build the environment can locate and change a named record and identify who holds each administrative credential using only the pack
revisit_triggers: any configuration change made during the project or the stabilization window
a handover question the pack could not answer

nodes.definition: Close the project with an explicit acceptance event rather than letting it fade into open-ended support. The gate has conditions: the verification checklist is complete, the stabilization window has closed, the as-built pack has been delivered and walked through, credential custody has been confirmed by the client actually signing in with the credential they hold, the recoverability statement has been acknowledged, the findings register including its declines has been reviewed, the decision about decommissioning the source system has been made in writing, and the boundary between project work and the recurring service has been stated so both sides know what is billable from tomorrow. Acceptance is the moment the client's ownership of their own environment becomes a demonstrated fact rather than a claim, and it is the clean hand-off point into the subscription and support relationship that follows.

included: the dated acceptance checklist and who signed for the client
credential custody proven by the client using their own credential
a walkthrough of the documentation pack
acknowledgement of the recoverability statement and review of the findings register
the written source-decommission decision
the stated boundary between project work and the recurring service
excluded: the recurring service's scope, cadence and commercial terms
renewal and true-up administration
any new project work, which is scoped and priced separately

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a post-acceptance dispute, or an item found still open after sign-off

pros.claim: A dated acceptance with a proven client credential ends the project cleanly and proves the client owns what they paid for
pros.example: the owner signs in with their own administrative credential during the handover meeting, so ownership is demonstrated rather than asserted

pros.claim: Stating the project-to-service boundary at acceptance prevents the slow bleed of unbilled work that follows an unclear ending
pros.example: both sides leave the meeting knowing that new user setups from next week are service work rather than project work

cons.claim: Pushing for formal acceptance can feel like chasing a signature while small items remain open, and a rigid gate can stall on something trivial
cons.example: acceptance delayed a fortnight over one user's mobile profile while the rest of the business works happily

failure_modes: having no acceptance event at all, so the project never ends and support expectations are set by accident
accepting while the source system is already gone and something is still missing
handing over documentation without confirming the client can actually use the credentials it describes
acceptance_tests: a dated acceptance record lists each condition met, names who signed for the client, and states the project-to-service boundary
the client has demonstrably used the administrative credential they hold, and the source-decommission decision is recorded in writing
revisit_triggers: an open item is discovered after acceptance
the client disputes what was in scope for the project

edges.why_related: discovery reads consoles and exports that only documented, authorized access makes lawful and defensible
the handling rules operate inside the scope the authorization record defines, and cannot be narrower or broader than it
discovery names the domains, the registrar and the DNS host whose custody then has to be proven
the account model is designed from the real mailbox census, role addresses and permission map rather than from headcount
separating administrative identities is how least privilege is actually implemented inside the tenant
administrative and break-glass accounts are created within the naming and account model the architecture fixes
enforcement can only be switched on safely once separate admin identities and an excluded break-glass account exist
the wider hardening set assumes a second factor is already enforced and legacy sign-in paths are closed
recoverability is designed against the residual loss scenarios the baseline does not already prevent
authorization, signing and policy records can only be published by whoever demonstrably controls the zone
fidelity is a property of the chosen method and tool, so the scope statement is written after the method is fixed
the pilot tests the fidelity claims the scope statement makes before the whole business relies on them
the pilot must run against the hardened tenant so that any conflict between the tool and enforcement appears early
the runbook's timings, step order and per-user steps come from what the pilot actually measured
the runbook's record-change order and device re-point steps are drawn from the sender and authentication design
what users are told to do and when comes straight out of the runbook's freeze window and per-user steps
execution is the runbook performed, and its verification checks are the runbook's pass criteria
the rollback trigger and point of no return defined in the runbook are what make a way back meaningful
users are set up and taught on an environment that has already been proven to send and receive
the stabilization window starts from the verification result and inherits its open lines
the pack records the environment as verified after cutover, not as designed before it
acceptance requires a delivered, walked-through pack the client holds
the migration tool's access model, its service account and where staged data lands are all bounded by the least-privilege rules
a method that depends on an authentication path or consent the baseline forbids is not available, whatever its cost advantage
no window may be scheduled until control of the zone has been proven and time-to-live reduction has been applied
a backup add-on may only be proposed against an identified exposure and with the included native capabilities stated plainly
closing legacy authentication paths breaks migration tools and protocols that rely on a stored password
edges.resolution_rule: keep tenant-wide enforcement and grant only a scoped, time-boxed exception for the named migration account, recorded in the exception register with an expiry no later than cutover; if no such exception is acceptable, change the migration method rather than weakening enforcement for users

edges.why_related: schedule pressure pushes toward passing the point of no return, while continuity demands the way back is kept open
edges.resolution_rule: business continuity dominates the schedule: the window does not open without a written rollback trigger and a reachable source, and the point of no return is only crossed when the runbook's stated pass criteria have been met

edges.why_related: the fidelity the client wants can exceed what the cheapest viable method can deliver
edges.resolution_rule: never promise fidelity the chosen method cannot deliver: either change the method and re-price the work, or record the exclusion in the fidelity statement and obtain the client's acknowledgement before any mailbox moves

edges.why_related: baseline work exposes gaps at the moment the client is most anxious and most likely to buy whatever is suggested
edges.resolution_rule: fix inside the project only what blocks safe delivery of the agreed scope; record every other finding neutrally with its materiality and defer it to the scheduled review, and never use a threat framing that is not supported by an observed finding in this tenant

edges.why_related: the appetite to clean up a decade of folder sprawl competes directly with the hours the mail cutover needs
edges.resolution_rule: the cutover date wins: only remediation that blocks transfer (illegal characters, over-long paths, locked files) happens inside the window, and discretionary restructuring is quoted and scheduled as separate work after acceptance

edges.why_related: fast triage under pressure tempts the technician toward standing high privilege and toward reading mailbox content
edges.resolution_rule: privilege is escalated per incident, time-boxed and logged with the reason, and mailbox content is opened only so far as reproducing the specific reported fault requires; speed never justifies standing global rights or browsing beyond the reported item

edges.why_related: most post-cutover incidents trace back to something the inventory never captured, so discovery quality drives the stabilization load
what users were told, and by whom, largely determines how many of the first week's contacts are genuine faults rather than surprise
time-to-live reduction has to be applied at least one previous time-to-live period before the record change, or caches will keep sending mail to the old system after the switch
dates and per-user instructions are announced to staff only after the pilot has measured what the window really takes
fixes and configuration changes made during stabilization must flow back into the pack or it becomes a false map
a failed delivery test or a device that cannot relay re-opens the sender authorization and flow design rather than being patched around
both are the people-facing half of delivery, drawing on the same internal champion and the same plain-language material, and they succeed or fail for the same reasons

conflict_axes.name: cutover_speed_vs_verified_readiness
conflict_axes.description: The client wants the promised date and the reseller wants the job finished, but pilot measurement, verification and a proven rollback position all take time the schedule resents.
poles: cut over on the promised date
cut over only when measurement, verification and rollback are proven
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: let readiness criteria rather than the calendar open the window; if the criteria are unmet, move the date and say why in writing, because a missed date costs far less than lost mail

conflict_axes.name: security_baseline_strictness_vs_user_friction
conflict_axes.description: Every hardening step that closes a real attack path also breaks a habit, a device or a workflow somebody depends on.
poles: enforce the full baseline immediately
soften the baseline to keep users comfortable
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep the baseline intact and absorb the friction through sequencing, training and a scoped exception register with expiry dates, rather than by lowering the standard

conflict_axes.name: reseller_admin_convenience_vs_client_ownership
conflict_axes.description: It is faster for the reseller to hold every credential and administer directly, but that leaves the client unable to leave, unable to act in an emergency and dependent on one supplier.
poles: reseller holds all administrative access
client owns the tenant and holds their own credential
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: client ownership always wins: work through revocable delegated access, ensure the client holds an administrative credential they have actually used, and document custody in the handover pack

conflict_axes.name: migration_fidelity_vs_window_and_budget
conflict_axes.description: Carrying every rule, permission, category and archive perfectly costs method complexity, tool licensing and hours that a fixed setup fee does not contain.
poles: move everything at full fidelity
move what the business needs inside the agreed window
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: decide fidelity per data class against business need, write the exclusions into a statement the client acknowledges, and price any upgrade in fidelity as a change rather than absorbing it silently

conflict_axes.name: lift_and_shift_vs_clean_rebuild
conflict_axes.description: Carrying the existing mess across is quick and familiar; rebuilding it cleanly is better forever but adds change at the moment users are least receptive.
poles: replicate the current environment as-is
rebuild to a clean standard model
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: rebuild only what would be expensive or impossible to change later - identity model, naming, shared mailboxes, permission groups - and carry the rest across unchanged for a later, separately scheduled cleanup

conflict_axes.name: legacy_sender_compatibility_vs_authentication_hygiene
conflict_axes.description: The copier, the alarm panel and the ten-year-old line-of-business application all want to send mail the way they always have, while authentication hygiene requires that only known, authorized systems can send as the domain.
poles: keep every legacy sender working as it is
authorize and authenticate every sender strictly
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: enumerate senders first, give each one a supported path (authenticated submission, an authorized relay, or its own subdomain), and tighten policy only after monitoring shows the inventory is complete

conflict_axes.name: documented_authorization_vs_expedient_access
conflict_axes.description: Written authorization and least-privilege escalation slow the first hours and the worst hours, exactly when everyone wants the technician to just fix it.
poles: act now on a verbal request
act only within documented, logged authorization
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: documented authorization dominates: use a fast written path such as an email confirmation from the authorizing officer, but never substitute urgency for a record, and never open content beyond the reported fault

conflict_axes.name: observed_need_vs_revenue_temptation
conflict_axes.description: Onboarding reveals genuine gaps at the moment the client is most anxious, which is precisely when an add-on sale is easiest and least trustworthy.
poles: sell the fix while the fear is fresh
record the finding neutrally and defer to the scheduled review
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: only fixes that block safe delivery of the agreed scope happen now; everything else goes into the findings register with observed evidence and materiality and is decided at the review, with declines recorded and respected

conflict_axes.name: bounded_hypercare_vs_open_ended_goodwill
conflict_axes.description: Generosity after cutover builds enormous goodwill and also silently converts a fixed-fee project into unlimited free support.
poles: help with everything for as long as it takes
hold the stated window and its scope
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: state the window and its scope in writing before cutover, be genuinely generous inside it, close it explicitly, and route everything after it through the recurring arrangement

conflict_axes.name: one_standard_baseline_vs_per_client_bespoke
conflict_axes.description: A single repeatable baseline is what makes a one-person reseller able to run many tenants safely, while each client has a workflow that wants an exception.
poles: apply the identical standard everywhere
tailor each tenant to its client
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep one baseline and one deviation register: exceptions are allowed but must be written down with a reason, an owner and a date so the standard stays visible and auditable

edge_cases.description: The client cannot produce registrar credentials because the domain was registered years ago by a web developer who has since disappeared or wound up their company
edge_cases.trigger: nobody at the client can log in to the registrar, and the registrant contact is an old third-party address
edge_cases.mitigation: start the registrar's documented recovery or transfer process immediately, do not offer any cutover date until control is proven, and if the domain proves unrecoverable treat a domain change as a separate business decision for the client with its own communication plan

edge_cases.description: What the client calls a shared mailbox turns out to be one licensed account that three staff sign in to with the same password
edge_cases.trigger: discovery finds a single account with several people's devices and no individual attribution
edge_cases.mitigation: convert to individual accounts plus a shared mailbox with granted permissions, explain the auditing and second-factor reasons to the owner, and schedule the change with the migration rather than after it

edge_cases.description: One mailbox or archive is far larger than the rest and will not fit the planned window, or a single desktop archive file is enormous
edge_cases.trigger: the census shows one or two mailboxes dominating total volume, or a very large archive file is found on a workstation
edge_cases.mitigation: pre-stage the heavy mailbox well ahead, split it by archive date, or move it as a separate wave; record the split in the fidelity statement and never let one mailbox dictate the whole business's window

edge_cases.description: A copier, alarm panel or line-of-business application sends mail as the domain and nobody knows its credentials or who configured it
edge_cases.trigger: discovery or authentication reports show a sender that no person at the client can account for
edge_cases.mitigation: trace the sender through mail logs and reports, give it a supported authenticated path with a dedicated account before any policy is tightened, and verify it with a test message inside the cutover window

edge_cases.description: The owner refuses to use a second factor while being the single most targeted account in the business
edge_cases.trigger: the authorizing officer asks to be excluded from enforcement because it is inconvenient
edge_cases.mitigation: offer the lowest-friction supported method, explain the exposure using what was observed in their own environment rather than a generic scare, and if the refusal stands record it as a dated exception with an expiry and a written acknowledgement rather than quietly weakening the tenant

edge_cases.description: The only available cutover weekend collides with payroll, month-end, a filing deadline or the client's seasonal peak
edge_cases.trigger: the business calendar check finds the proposed window sits on a critical business event
edge_cases.mitigation: move the window, or if the date is immovable split the migration into waves that leave the critical function untouched until after the event, and confirm the choice in writing with the authorizing officer

edge_cases.description: The source is a consumer-grade or free mail service whose export and access capabilities are limited, throttled or being retired
edge_cases.trigger: the chosen migration tool cannot obtain the access it needs, or transfers run far slower than planned
edge_cases.mitigation: measure the real limit in the pilot, fall back to a per-user export and import path with an explicit fidelity note, and re-size the window and the communication before promising anything

edge_cases.description: A departing employee's mailbox must be preserved untouched because of a dispute or an investigation while the migration is under way
edge_cases.trigger: the client discloses a legal matter, or asks for one mailbox to be frozen
edge_cases.mitigation: leave that mailbox in place, apply the platform's hold capability class after verifying its current behaviour, keep the source copy reachable, log every access, and tell the client to take their own legal advice on the obligation class involved

edge_cases.description: DNS is managed by a third-party web host who applies changes slowly, in business hours only, or overwrites the zone during unrelated site work
edge_cases.trigger: the DNS custody check shows the change path runs through an unresponsive or careless third party
edge_cases.mitigation: agree the change ticket and its timing with that host in advance, or move DNS hosting to a console the client controls before the window; keep a zone export so an overwrite can be reversed quickly

edge_cases.description: After cutover some users keep working in the old system, so conversations split across two mailboxes and replies vanish from colleagues' view
edge_cases.trigger: the stabilization log shows mail still arriving in or being sent from the source system
edge_cases.mitigation: identify the users, remove the old profile from their devices, keep the source read-only for retrieval only, and reinforce with the champion that the old system is no longer a place to work

edge_cases.description: The migration tool reports complete success but a delegate or send-as permission set never carried, and it is discovered days later by the person who needed it
edge_cases.trigger: a user reports they cannot open or send from a mailbox they always could
edge_cases.mitigation: treat permission rebuild as a manual list verified per user inside the window rather than as tool output, and add the missed case to the verification checklist so it cannot recur on the next migration

edge_cases.description: A manager asks the reseller directly to give them access to another employee's mailbox, or to forward it, without going through the authorizing officer
edge_cases.trigger: an access request arrives from somebody who is not on the approved-requester list, often framed as urgent
edge_cases.mitigation: decline politely, route the request to the authorizing officer for written approval, execute only what that approval covers, and file the approval with the change record; never act on urgency alone

workflow.action: Establish written authorization, the access model and the data-handling limits
workflow.description: Name the authorizing officer and approved requesters, record the in-scope domains, systems and mailboxes, agree delegated revocable access rather than shared passwords, and state client ownership of tenant and data
workflow.gate: the record is dated before any administrative action and names the officer, the requesters, the scope, the access model and how it is revoked

workflow.action: Inventory the source environment from consoles rather than from memory
workflow.description: Export the mailbox census with sizes and types, map permissions, aliases and lists, enumerate every device and application that sends as the domain, locate files and archives, and list credential holders
workflow.gate: mailbox census reconciles against the source console, and every sending device or application has a named owner and a current sending method

workflow.action: Prove domain and DNS control and prepare the zone
workflow.description: Confirm registrant, registrar and DNS host custody, export the zone and label each record keep, change or retire, perform a test change, and lower time-to-live on the records that will change
workflow.gate: a test record has been added and removed by the party who will run the cutover, and reduced time-to-live values are live well before the window

workflow.action: Design the tenant and identity model before creating any account
workflow.description: Fix the creation-time choices knowingly, verify the client domain and make it primary, and settle per-human accounts, shared and resource mailboxes, groups, licence assignment and the naming standard
workflow.gate: the domain is verified and primary, and every planned account, shared mailbox, resource account and group appears with its purpose and naming pattern before the first account is created

workflow.action: Separate administrative identities and create the break-glass account
workflow.description: Create distinct admin identities, establish the client-held administrative credential and its custody, create and exclude the break-glass account, configure alerting on its use, and scope the reseller's delegated access
workflow.gate: a named client officer holds an administrative credential, the break-glass account is excluded and alerted, and the reseller's access is demonstrably revocable

workflow.action: Enrol, enforce and verify multi-factor authentication and close legacy sign-in paths
workflow.description: Choose methods with a documented fallback, enrol administrators first, run the registration window to an announced enforcement date, close or scope legacy authentication, and verify from sign-in data
workflow.gate: every enabled account has a registered factor or a dated exception with an owner, and sign-in data shows no successful legacy-authentication sign-ins for in-scope accounts

workflow.action: Publish the sender authorization, signing and monitoring policy
workflow.description: Consolidate authorization for every enumerated sender, enable and publish signing, start reporting policy in monitoring mode, and assign each device and application a supported sending path
workflow.gate: one valid authorization record resolves within the lookup limits, signing verifies on a test message, and monitoring reports show only known senders before any tightening

workflow.action: Select the migration method and write the data scope and fidelity statement
workflow.description: Score the candidate methods against source capability, volume, throughput and interruption tolerance, prove the tool's required access, then write the per-class in-or-out decision, fidelity notes and manual rebuild list
workflow.artifact: migration plan with acknowledged fidelity statement
workflow.gate: the chosen method is recorded with its reasoning and proven tool access, and the client has acknowledged in writing what will not move

workflow.action: Run the pilot on a representative cohort and measure
workflow.description: Migrate the champion plus a heavy mailbox, a shared mailbox, a delegated case and an awkward device; measure throughput and per-user setup time; verify fidelity; log and fold back every issue
workflow.gate: measured throughput and setup time are recorded, fidelity is confirmed against the statement, and every issue is fixed in the runbook or explicitly accepted before scheduling

workflow.action: Write the cutover runbook, schedule it against the business calendar and send the user communications
workflow.description: Build the timed sequence with owners, pass criteria, freeze instruction, record-change order, point of no return, rollback trigger and on-call contacts, confirm the date against payroll and seasonal constraints, and release the announcement and reminder messages from a client-side sender
workflow.artifact: cutover runbook and client communication pack
workflow.gate: every step has an owner, a duration and a pass criterion, the window is confirmed in writing by the authorizing officer, and the announcement and reminder have gone out with per-user prerequisites complete

workflow.action: Execute the cutover and verify delivery per user and per system
workflow.description: Complete the delta pass, change records in the planned order, check propagation from several vantage points, then test two-way external mail, auto-configuration, device relays, mobile profiles, shared mailboxes and delegate access
workflow.gate: each migrated user, each shared mailbox and each sending device has an individually ticked pass, and no verification line was skipped

workflow.action: Train users, run the stabilization window, then document and accept
workflow.description: Complete per-user setup and the high-frequency training, run the stated stabilization window to its communicated close, finish the as-built pack including credential custody, review the findings register, decide on source decommission, and hold the acceptance meeting
workflow.artifact: as-built pack plus dated acceptance record
workflow.gate: the stabilization window is closed in writing, the client holds and has used their own administrative credential, the decommission decision is recorded, and the project-to-service boundary is stated and signed

priority_rationale: Authorization and least-privilege handling come first because every later action is only legitimate inside them; discovery, proven DNS control and the tenant and identity architecture follow because they fix the facts and the creation-time choices that everything downstream inherits; the security baseline, multi-factor enforcement, recoverability design and mail authentication are built next because a tenant must be safe and able to deliver before data lands in it; method selection, data scope, file migration and the pilot then convert those facts into a measured plan; the runbook, user communication, execution with per-user verification and the rollback position carry the business across without interruption; and training, stabilization, honest findings disclosure, as-built documentation and a dated acceptance close the project so the client demonstrably owns the environment they paid for.

dominance_rules.rule: Documented client authorization dominates operational convenience and urgency
dominance_rules.rationale: administrative access to a business's mail is a fiduciary-grade responsibility, and urgency is the framing every improper access request arrives in
dominance_rules.trigger: any request to access, forward, export or grant rights over a mailbox or file store, however urgent it sounds
dominance_rules.action: route the request to the authorizing officer, act only within the written approval obtained, and file that approval with the change record

dominance_rules.rule: Client ownership of the tenant dominates reseller administrative convenience
dominance_rules.rationale: a client who cannot reach their own tenant is exposed to supplier failure and is locked in against their will, which no efficiency gain justifies
dominance_rules.trigger: any decision about who holds credentials, who owns the tenant, or how the reseller's access is granted
dominance_rules.action: keep the tenant in the client's ownership, ensure a named client officer holds and has used an administrative credential, and use revocable delegated access for the reseller

dominance_rules.rule: Business mail continuity dominates the cutover schedule
dominance_rules.rationale: a missed date is an inconvenience while lost or undelivered mail is a business injury that can end the relationship
dominance_rules.trigger: readiness criteria are unmet as the scheduled window approaches
dominance_rules.action: move the window and explain why in writing rather than opening it without a proven rollback position and a completed delta pass

dominance_rules.rule: Proven DNS control dominates any promised cutover date
dominance_rules.rationale: a cutover is a record change, so without demonstrated control of the zone the date is an aspiration and not a plan
dominance_rules.trigger: a date is requested or offered before a test change has been performed by the party who will run the cutover
dominance_rules.action: withhold the date until custody is proven and reduced time-to-live values are live, and put the recovery of control on the critical path

dominance_rules.rule: Identity hardening dominates user convenience, with exceptions only when scoped, recorded and time-limited
dominance_rules.rationale: an unprotected mailbox in a small business is the standard route to invoice fraud and supplier impersonation, and permanent exceptions become permanent exposure
dominance_rules.trigger: a user, including the owner, asks to be excluded from enforcement, or a device cannot support the standard
dominance_rules.action: offer the lowest-friction supported method, and if an exception is unavoidable record it with an owner, a reason and an expiry rather than weakening the tenant

dominance_rules.rule: Data preservation dominates cleanup, cost saving and schedule
dominance_rules.rationale: deletion and decommission are the only truly irreversible actions in a migration, and a month of duplicated subscription is trivial beside permanent data loss
dominance_rules.trigger: any proposal to delete a mailbox, wipe a server or cancel the source subscription
dominance_rules.action: hold until acceptance, reconciliation, a client-held export and written approval are all evidenced

dominance_rules.rule: Observed need dominates revenue opportunity in every recommendation
dominance_rules.rationale: trust compounds across the years of a subscription relationship while a pressured sale earns once and poisons the account
dominance_rules.trigger: a security or licensing gap is discovered during onboarding and an add-on could be sold on the strength of it
dominance_rules.action: record the finding neutrally with its materiality, state what the current subscription already covers, fix only what blocks safe delivery now, and defer the rest to the scheduled review

dominance_rules.rule: Least-privilege content access dominates troubleshooting speed
dominance_rules.rationale: the reseller's standing to hold administrative rights rests entirely on not using them beyond the task at hand
dominance_rules.trigger: an incident tempts the technician toward standing high privilege or toward browsing mailbox content
dominance_rules.action: escalate privilege per incident with a time box and a logged reason, and open only the content the specific reported fault requires

dominance_rules.rationale: migration tools report their own completion, not whether a person can actually send from the shared address on Monday morning
dominance_rules.trigger: a tool or console reports success and there is pressure to close the window
dominance_rules.action: require the two-way delivery test, the device relay test and the per-user tick before the window is declared closed

anti_rework_rules.rule: Prove domain and DNS control before offering any cutover date
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a promised date collapsing when it emerges that a former web developer holds the registrar, forcing rescheduling and lost client confidence

anti_rework_rules.rule: Complete the source inventory before selecting a migration method or writing a scope
anti_rework_rules.prevents: choosing a method that cannot carry a data class or a mailbox size nobody had measured, and re-planning the whole migration mid-flight

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide the identity, sign-in-name and naming model before creating the first account
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a rename campaign that breaks logins, permissions, saved profiles and every mail client after the tenant is already populated

anti_rework_rules.rule: Create separate administrative identities and an excluded break-glass account before enforcing multi-factor
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a policy change locking the administrators out of the tenant they are configuring, with no emergency path back in

anti_rework_rules.rule: Enumerate every device and application that sends as the domain before publishing or tightening any authentication policy
anti_rework_rules.prevents: silently killing legitimate mail from a copier, an invoicing package or a reminder service and hunting the cause for weeks

anti_rework_rules.rule: Lower time-to-live on the records that will change well before the window, never during it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: mail continuing to reach the old system for hours after the switch because caches still hold the previous value

anti_rework_rules.rule: Run the pilot and fold its findings back into the runbook before scheduling the production window
anti_rework_rules.prevents: committing a whole business to a window sized by assumption, then discovering the throughput and per-user setup time were wrong

anti_rework_rules.rule: Get the fidelity statement acknowledged in writing before the first mailbox moves
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a Monday-morning dispute about rules, permissions or archives that were never in scope but were also never disclosed

anti_rework_rules.rule: Write the as-built documentation as each component is configured rather than from memory at the end
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a handover pack that is wrong in the details that matter, and a later technician working from a false map of the environment

iteration_protocol.trigger: pilot throughput, fidelity or per-user setup time diverges materially from the plan
iteration_protocol.action: re-size the window, re-select the method if necessary, update the fidelity statement, and re-issue dates to users before anything else proceeds

iteration_protocol.trigger: an undocumented device or application that sends as the domain is discovered after authentication records were published
iteration_protocol.action: add it to the sender inventory, give it a supported authenticated path, re-publish the consolidated record, and hold any policy tightening until monitoring is clean again

iteration_protocol.trigger: a lockout or a bypass is reported around the enforcement date
iteration_protocol.action: confirm the break-glass exclusion still holds, re-check the exception register and its expiries, re-sequence enrolment for the affected group, and verify again from sign-in data

iteration_protocol.trigger: stabilization tickets cluster into a systematic class such as missing permissions, unmigrated archives or devices still on the old server
iteration_protocol.action: run a targeted remediation pass for the whole class rather than case by case, then update the verification checklist, the training and the discovery inventory so the class cannot recur

iteration_protocol.trigger: DNS control changes hands, or a record is overwritten by a third party during unrelated work
iteration_protocol.action: re-verify custody, restore the records from the zone export, re-test delivery and authentication, and update the custody map in the documentation pack

iteration_protocol.trigger: the vendor changes a plan capability, a retention window, an enforcement default or the delegated-administration mechanism
iteration_protocol.action: re-verify the affected mechanism against current vendor documentation for this client's plan, adjust the baseline and the recoverability statement, and record the change in the documentation pack

iteration_protocol.trigger: acceptance is refused, or the documentation pack cannot answer a question asked during handover
iteration_protocol.action: reopen the specific gap, correct the pack, re-run the affected verification, and hold acceptance until the condition genuinely passes rather than waiving it

iteration_protocol.trigger: a security or licensing gap is observed during onboarding that is not needed for safe delivery of the agreed scope
iteration_protocol.action: record it in the findings register with observed evidence and materiality, state what the current subscription already covers, and carry it to the scheduled review instead of raising it under cutover pressure
